mutations.because: D43's one-composed-frame invariant, broken the way this lane makes it easy to break. The guard that used to hold it (`presentation !== "guided" || the step is not review/layout`) existed because two other surfaces carried a frame of their own -- Review's figure and the Layout STEP's `preview`. SG1 deletes Review and the steps, so the guard goes, and what keeps the count at one is now a single omitted prop on ONE line of the column. Adding it back is the most plausible thing a later lane does: `preview` is LayoutSection's own documented capability (T7/D63), it reads as restoring something the wizard had, and D141's comment used to say the exclusion survived "in every presentation". Nothing looks wrong: two real creatives, both correct, both fed the same projection, every `getByRole`/`getByText` in the suite satisfied -- a SECOND frame passes every query that looks for one. It is caught only by a count of MOUNTS (`data-testid="preview-frame"`, CC1's marker, present in both branches PreviewFrame can render), because the rail's container query hides without unmounting and happy-dom applies no CSS at all, so a visible-node count would be the wrong question. (Re-anchored by ANCHORS: the recorded text was reformatted or moved, not changed — the mutation, its claim and its command are untouched.)
command: exactly one composed frame is mounted

mutations.because: `reveal`'s two halves deliberately point at DIFFERENT things for motion, and this collapses them into one. Motion is a bucket with no section of its own: the scroll must reach `#motion` (the panel inside Output, where the field the user has to fix actually is), while focus goes to the HOST section, because a `<section>` is what the handoff can make focusable. Unifying them looks like removing a duplicated ternary -- the two lines even read as though one of them forgot to map -- and for every non-motion bucket the two are identical, so the whole suite stays green except the one test that drives a Motion chip. The cost is silent and specific: the operator presses "Motion" on a refusal and lands on the top of Output instead of on the motion controls, with nothing to say it moved at all.
command: the Motion chip scrolls to the motion controls

mutations.because: SG1's whole reveal contract: with no steps left to change, `reveal` IS the scroll -- and this drops it, keeping only the focus handoff. It is the plausible simplification, not a random deletion: `focusSection` calls `focus({ preventScroll: true })` and its own comment says "the scroll above already placed it", so a reader who removes the scroll believes focus will do the placing. In a real browser a focus without `preventScroll` very nearly would, which is exactly why this survives a visual check. It leaves every reveal from a CHIP silently inert (chips are scroll-only, `focus` defaults false), so a refusal names a section the page never moves to. Caught by the chip test, which asserts the scroll ran ONCE and on the section element itself -- not merely that something scrolled.
command: an ErrorStrip chip scrolls its section in the column

mutations.because: The other half of D43's count, reintroduced as a plausible tidy-up. With the step gate gone the `<aside>` is unconditional, and `isRailWideEnough` sits right there looking like the condition that belongs on it -- the rail is CSS-hidden below the breakpoint anyway, so gating the mount too reads as saving a render. It is wrong for the reason CC2 wrote that flag: the rail must stay MOUNTED below the breakpoint so a resize back above it does not pay a fresh debounce, and `isRailWideEnough` gates only the `brief` prop (the FETCH). Every fetch-count proof stays green under this -- withholding the brief and unmounting the dock both produce zero calls -- and so does every test that looks at the rail at a normal width. Caught only by the test that narrows `window.innerWidth` and then requires the landmark to still be there.
command: nothing fetches below the breakpoint, though the rail still mounts
mutations.retired: Retired by ANCHORS: the subject is reshaped and, as SG4's remediation and the rail-in-the-shell plan both recorded, its own assertion no longer moves. `railSlot` is a `useCallback` returning a `<div>`; the `<aside>` this mutation gates is published by the shell, so an aside-presence assertion cannot see the gate any more. The property — the rail stays MOUNTED below the breakpoint so a resize pays no fresh debounce — is carried instead by rs.json#12, which says in its own `because` that it carries it rather than re-authoring this one.

mutations.because: The gate SG1 narrowed, widened the other way. It used to read `mode === "variation" && presentation === "everything"`, and the `presentation` term was what kept the sidebar accordion from doubling the Guided policy STEP; this lane drops that term and leaves the mode alone. Making it unconditional is the tempting next step -- "why hide a panel?" -- and it is wrong because `sectionOrder("brief")` has no `policy` at all: a Classic brief has no variation policy to set, so the panel would offer axis controls for a block `toBrief` never emits, and every press would edit state the projection drops. Nothing throws and nothing looks broken: the accordion renders, its controls work, and a `getByRole` for it succeeds in both modes. Caught by the half of the policy test that asserts an ABSENCE after a flip to Classic -- the presence half alone would pass.
command: the policy sidebar renders for a variation brief
